summary: A yes/no question is the statement with هَلْ in front and the Arabic question mark ؟ at the end; the word order does not change and there is no helper verb: تُحِبُّ الشَّايَ → هَلْ تُحِبُّ الشَّايَ؟ (Do you like tea?). Before al- هَلْ takes a helping vowel: هَلِ الطِّفْلُ يَشْرَبُ الْحَلِيبَ؟. The prefix أَ, written together with the first word, is the formal alternative (أَتَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ؟) and the only one before a negation (أَلَا تُحِبُّ …؟، أَلَيْسَ …؟). “Or” in a choice question (which one?) is أَمْ: أَتُرِيدُ شَايًا أَمْ قَهْوَةً؟; أَوْ asks “any of them?” (هَلْ تُرِيدُ سُكَّرًا أَوْ حَلِيبًا؟ — answer yes / no). Answers: نَعَمْ (yes), لَا (no), and بَلَى “yes, it is so” against a negative question — the Arabic doch. Short answers: رُبَّمَا (maybe), طَبْعًا (of course), حَقًّا؟ (really?); add أَيْضًا (too) or فَقَطْ (only) after the word they belong to.

askYourself: Is it a yes/no question (not who / what / where)? → هَلْ + the unchanged statement + ؟
Does the next word start with al-? → هَلِ with a helping vowel: هَلِ الطِّفْلُ …؟
Is the question negative (don’t you …? isn’t it …?) → أَ, not هَلْ: أَلَا …؟ أَلَيْسَ …؟
Am I offering a choice (this one or that one)? → أَمْ (أَ … أَمْ …؟). Asking “any of them?” → أَوْ.
Answering a negative question with “yes, it is / I do”? → بَلَى, not نَعَمْ.
Did I write the Arabic question mark ؟ ?

traps: No inversion and no “do”: هَلْ تُرِيدُ قَهْوَةً؟ = do you want a coffee?
Do not combine هَلْ with a question word: *هَلْ أَيْنَ …؟
Not *هَلْ لَا …: a negative question takes أَ — أَلَا تُحِبُّ …؟
أَ is written together with the next word: أَتُرِيدُ, not *أَ تُرِيدُ.
To a negative question, “yes, I do” is بَلَى, not نَعَمْ.
أَمْ (or) is not أُمّ (mother): ʾam / ʾumm.
Before al-: هَلِ، أَوِ، أَمِ (helping vowel i).

seeAlso.note: Hebrew marks a yes/no question with הַאִם in writing or only with intonation in speech — the same idea as هَلْ; its old prefix הֲ־ is the cousin of Arabic أَ.
German moves the verb to the front (Trinkst du Tee?) and answers a negative question with doch — Arabic never changes the order, adds هَلْ, and says بَلَى for doch.
Chinese adds 吗 at the end where Arabic puts هَلْ at the start; Chinese 还是 is Arabic أَمْ (a choice), 或者 is أَوْ.

blocks.caption: The order of the words does not change — you only add هَلْ (or أَ) and ؟.

items.title: أَمْ — which one?
points: careful style: أَ … أَمْ; modern writing also هَلْ … أَمْ

items.title: أَوْ — any of them?
points: also the “or” of statements: آكُلُ السَّمَكَ أَوِ الدَّجَاجَ

means
when
rows: agrees with the question as asked
denies it; followed by a pause: لَا، شُكْرًا
contradicts a negative question: أَلَا تُحِبُّ الشَّايَ؟ بَلَى! — German doch
surprise: عِنْدِي أَحَدَ عَشَرَ أَخًا. حَقًّا؟

blocks.title: Yes to a negative question.
blocks.text: أَلَا تُحِبُّ الشَّايَ؟ — نَعَمْ means “right, I don’t”; بَلَى means “yes I do”. Just like German Magst du keinen Tee? — Doch!

blocks.title: Too and only come after.
blocks.text: أَنَا أَيْضًا أُحِبُّ السَّمَكَ (I like fish too) — أَيْضًا follows the word it adds to. أَشْرَبُ الْمَاءَ فَقَطْ (I only drink water) — فَقَطْ follows the word it limits.
In speech many people drop هَلْ and ask with the voice alone (تُرِيدُ شَايًا؟ ↗); in writing هَلْ or أَ is expected. Wh-questions (what, where …) never take هَلْ: that is lesson 10.

quiz.why: هَلْ in front, the statement unchanged, ؟ at the end.

quiz.q: “Do you want tea or coffee?” (which one?)

quiz.why: Before a negation only أَ is used.
بَلَى contradicts the negative question, like German doch; نَعَمْ would confirm “it isn’t”.
A helping vowel i: هَلِ الطِّفْلُ يَشْرَبُ الْحَلِيبَ؟
أَيْضًا (too) follows the word it adds to (أَنَا); فَقَطْ would mean “only I”.

notes.text: Hindi क्या at the start of a yes/no question (क्या तुम चाय पीते हो?) is exactly Arabic هَلْ: the statement stays as it is.
Persian آیا at the start (آیا چای می‌خواهی؟) works like هَلْ; both are often dropped in speech, leaving only the voice.
Swahili Je, … ? at the start of a question (Je, unapenda chai?) works like هَلْ.
Greek asks with the voice alone (θέλεις τσάι;); Arabic adds هَلْ in front, and its question mark is ؟.
Russian asks with the voice, or with ли after the word in question (хочешь ли ты чаю?); Arabic puts هَلْ in front.
Spanish uses intonation and ¿…?; Arabic adds هَلْ at the start and writes ؟ only at the end.
English inverts or adds do (Do you like tea?); Arabic keeps the statement and adds هَلْ: هَلْ تُحِبُّ الشَّايَ؟ For “yes, I do” after a negative question it has a word of its own, بَلَى.
French est-ce que before an unchanged statement (est-ce que tu aimes le thé ?) is the idea of هَلْ; and French si — “yes, I do” after a negative question — is Arabic بَلَى.
Turkish puts mi after the word in question (çay istiyor musun?); Arabic puts هَلْ at the start of the sentence.
Japanese adds か at the end (お茶が好きですか); Arabic puts هَلْ at the start. Japanese はい after a negative question agrees with it, as Arabic نَعَمْ does; “yes, I do” is بَلَى.
Korean asks with the verb ending and the voice (좋아해요?); Arabic adds the separate word هَلْ.
Finnish -ko / -kö goes on the first word (Juotko teetä?); Arabic also marks the start of the sentence — with هَلْ, or the formal prefix أَ on the first word (أَتَشْرَبُ؟).
Hungarian asks with intonation alone (Iszol teát?); Arabic adds هَلْ in front.
Luganda asks yes/no questions with intonation; Arabic adds هَلْ.
Vietnamese wraps the verb in có … không? (bạn có uống trà không?); Arabic puts هَلْ in front and changes nothing else.
Inuktitut has a question mood inside the verb; Arabic adds the word هَلْ and leaves the verb as it is.
